RT @jun_song: The DGX Spark is not as durable as most people think.

Even official providers here in Korea are buying 1 spare unit for every 10 units they order, purely to handle warranty repairs.

These machines run very hot, and that heat is brutal on the unified memory. 

Because of how the board is built, you cannot just swap out dead RAM. You have to replace the entire motherboard.

If you are running a DGX Spark setup, take your cooling and thermal management very seriously.

tweets.content:
RT @Byron_Wan: I called it a whole year ago‼️

Megaspeed CEO Huang Xiaole (黄小乐) aka Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was found to be a Chinese intelligence asset funneling information to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. Surveillance of Alice Huang revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive.

The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Jensen Huang set off alarms at the White House.

Roughly a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.

American officials already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced AI chips.

But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the US has maintained in developing cutting-edge AI models.

Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services.

The surveillance of Alice Huang continues, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.

When Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, U.S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Jensen Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intel-gathering role for China.

The previous reporting about Alice Huang described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businesswoman and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade US prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips.

The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there.

Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department.

Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centers and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from Aivres, the US arm of 🇨🇳 Inspur, which has been blacklisted for funneling technology to the Chinese military, though Aivres remains free of sanctions.

Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. US officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run AI. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

1/n

https://t.co/W3CGceaJ7R

Two posts today. The one about an 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability got far more attention than the one about CAIRN/ARTEX.

I think the second topic is far more important.

I’ve been following vulnerabilities long enough to recognize the pattern. They’re discovered, exploited, patched, and replaced by the next ones. AI will accelerate this process dramatically, but the fundamental cycle remains the same.

What we’re seeing with AI-driven attack frameworks is something different. They’re starting to change how attacks are conducted in general, not just how vulnerabilities are discovered or exploited.

They allow attackers to plan, adapt, make decisions, and scale entire operations with far less human effort. And vulnerability exploitation is just a small part of what these systems can do.

I think this will have a much more profound and lasting impact on cybersecurity than the current wave of AI-discovered vulnerabilities.

Yet the individual CVE gets all the attention.

Linux kernel vulnerability:
https://t.co/YCrlvpmEqu

CAIRN/ARTEX:

quotedTweet.rawContent:
CVE-2026-98432 is a good example of something that really concerns me about the future of cybersecurity.

https://t.co/BJbXLKLFNq

The vulnerability was introduced in October 2015, more than 11 years ago, by a performance optimization in the Linux TCP/IPv4 networking stack. One of the most fundamental components of an operating system used by millions of servers.

Now Anthropic reports that Claude discovered this flaw and developed a working exploit that allows remote code execution as root, without authentication, against a server with an MPTCP listener.

https://t.co/j00p4TKS0a

Think about what that means.

For decades, we’ve been building critical infrastructure out of enormous amounts of complex, memory-unsafe code. Humans wrote it. Other humans reviewed it, tested it and searched for vulnerabilities. All working with the same fundamental limitations: limited time, limited attention, incomplete visibility and an inability to reason about every possible interaction and race condition.

And perhaps that’s what protected us to some extent. Attackers had the same limitations as the people developing and defending these systems.

A vulnerability could remain undiscovered for 11 years, even in such a widely used component.

Now AI is changing that balance.

The ability to inspect code, identify subtle weaknesses and develop working exploits is becoming less dependent on a small number of highly skilled researchers. These activities can increasingly be scaled with compute, automated testing and tokens.

And that’s what worries me about the next few years.

We’ve accumulated decades of complex, memory-unsafe code in operating systems, network services, applications and libraries. Much of it has never been assessed with anything close to the capabilities that are now becoming available.

We may have massively overestimated the security of our software simply because the people looking for vulnerabilities were as limited as the people who introduced them.

That balance is breaking down, and I don’t think we’re prepared for what follows.

tweets.content:
RT @sysxplore: Linux 7.4's networking changes are merged, sent in by Red Hat's Paolo Abeni.

The headline feature is hardware pacing offload. Instead of the CPU deciding exactly when each packet goes out, the network card handles that timing itself. Intel's IDPF driver is the first to support it.

Mixed BIG TCP paths get up to 70% more throughput, according to the pull request.

Meta's second-generation network card driver also lands upstream, so Meta keeps shipping drivers for its own data centre hardware straight into mainline.

And a proper Realtek driver replaces the old rtl8723bs one, which had been sitting in the kernel's staging area for less polished drivers.

The headline feature is hardware pacing offload. Instead of the CPU deciding exactly when each packet goes out, the network card handles that timing itself. Intel's IDPF driver is the first to support it.

Mixed BIG TCP paths get up to 70% more throughput, according to the pull request.

Meta's second-generation network card driver also lands upstream, so Meta keeps shipping drivers for its own data centre hardware straight into mainline.

And a proper Realtek driver replaces the old rtl8723bs one, which had been sitting in the kernel's staging area for less polished drivers.

RT @jun_song: In South Korea, a maxed-out Mac Studio M5 Ultra (512GB) is more expensive than a brand new Tesla Model Y.

In the US, the maxed M5 Ultra is around $30k, and a Model Y is $40k. Not even close.

Here in Korea, the numbers completely flip:
Mac Studio M5 Ultra: 50M KRW ($38k USD)
Tesla Model Y: 45M KRW ($34k USD)

Why does this happen?

First, Korea has some of the cheapest Tesla prices in the world. 
Tesla cut prices aggressively to match local EV subsidy limits and to fight domestic giants like Hyundai and Kia on their home turf.

Second, Apple seems to hate Korea. 
Even with zero import tariffs, Apple applies an absurdly high exchange rate that makes their hardware way overpriced here. 
What makes it worse is that the factories in China are right next door to Korea, so shipping costs are super low.

It is wild that a desktop computer costs more than an electric SUV.

Make your payload "sleep" to look like any real Windows activity.

BusyWork is a Rust library that swaps each pause for randomized real work - hashing, file enumeration, registry queries, DNS lookups - drawn from 76 tasks across seven categories with ±30% jitter on every parameter.

No two "pauses" produce the same API sequence, and no timing primitives survive in the compiled binary.

A post by Daniel (@PatchRequest)

RT @visegrad24: The Kremlin has ordered Apple and Microsoft to store and hand over Russian users’ data to security services

Roskomnadzor, Russia’s state censorship and communications watchdog, added Apple and Microsoft to the registry of information dissemination organizers.

Under the law, they must store data on users’ actions and communications inside Russia for three years and provide it, including the content of messages, to Russian special services on request.

For Apple, this could affect iMessage, FaceTime, iCloud Mail, AirDrop, shared albums, and notes. For Microsoft, it covers messaging, calling, and work services.

If the companies refuse to cooperate with the FSB, they face large fines in Russia and eventual blocking.

For some, this sounds like an astronomical cost. For others, it’s garden variety capex that will be written off against profits.

tweets.content:
agree! dont give developers or ai agents the ability to write insecure code in the first place. they are pressured to ship working features, security is someone else problem. this is also why "patch the planet" doesn't scale, no matter how hard you try.

xss is a pretty good example and probably decade long cat and mouse war against it is fascinating.

1. microsoft/early web designers makes mistake, mix data with executable code. what could possibly go wrong?
2. well, attacker controlled data runs as javascript. rise of xss.
3. microsoft be like, hmm, how do we stop this? let's make cookies not accessible to javascript. creates httponly cookies.
4. well, attacker runs javascript, they can do everything from the browser without stealing cookies
5. security people be like, educate developers, and patch patch patch.
6. samy worm spreads in myspace through xss
7. dang it, lets educate developers to not write insecure code, patch patch patch
8. wait, xss vulnerabilities are not getting exhausting rather raising like crazy, developers still writing insecure code.
9. browser security people decide to fix this once and for all. detect malicious input with heuristics(probably glorious regex? idk some boomer need to teach me how they used to work) and block it. microsoft creates xss filter, google follows with xss auditor.
10. well, parser differentials hit hard, attackers keep bypassing the filters, and the filters themselves introduce new vulnerabilities. google eventually kills xss auditor.
11. mozilla be like, these guys have skill issue. what if we context aware restrict which scripts can execute instead ? invents csp.
12. devs be like, hold my coffee. your security policy is breaking my feature. let me just allow everything, ship ship ship.
13. meanwhile, google and others think, why trust developers to escape everything correctly? build automatic escaping into frameworks.  rise of angular and react with secure defaults.
14. bahaha, still more xss. react literally calls its raw html escape hatch dangerouslySetInnerHTML, but dev uses it anyway cuz the feature works. ship it. (they did made rxss harder tho)
15. still more xss. reflected xss hasn't disappeared, and dom xss remains a problem.
16. google thinks harder. let's makes trusted types, lets make devs harder more, stop developers from passing arbitrary strings into dangerous dom sinks.
17. works kinda fine, but no one uses it except probably google and some others, there are probably devs at gogole who still use unsafe trusted policy 
18. so, google needs to make observability to catch developers that use it and shame
19. after 10 years, xss volumes goes down.
20. win

lesson?

you cant just patch your way out of this forever, fixing all bugs is a never ending cat and mouse game, you cant win this game at all.

you need make insecure code harder to write in the first place. reduce attack surface, and make dangerous operations difficult or impossible.

tweets.content:
RT @MarioNawfal: 🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Six days before the Iran strike window opens, Hegseth fired the general in charge of planning it

The Pentagon's chief planner on the Joint Staff, a three-star who commanded the 101st Airborne and carries six Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart, was pushed out this week with no explanation and no replacement named, the second man forced out of that job in a year. 

Officials told The Atlantic Hegseth lost confidence in him and he didn't get on with policy chief Elbridge Colby.

He's at least the fifth general removed this year and one of 26 generals and admirals gone since Hegseth arrived, after the Army chief of staff was fired at the height of the spring strikes while his service was supposed to be restocking the interceptors now in short supply.

One more detail: X users noticed that the general's son, a FEMA analyst, had written something offensive after Charlie Kirk's killing, named the father, and told Hegseth to "review" his employment.

The son was put on leave then; the father is out now. Whatever the reason, the job he held is the link between CENTCOM's strike options, Pentagon policy and the White House, and it's empty the week Trump decides between a deal and a week of bombing. 

Source: The Atlantic / Writer: Daniel

Back to revenue based pricing, reason it won't fly is that it is very hard to measure the ROI when you're the tool provider.

RT @visegrad24: The Kremlin has ordered Apple and Microsoft to store and hand over Russian users’ data to security services

Roskomnadzor, Russia’s state censorship and communications watchdog, added Apple and Microsoft to the registry of information dissemination organizers.

Under the law, they must store data on users’ actions and communications inside Russia for three years and provide it, including the content of messages, to Russian special services on request.

For Apple, this could affect iMessage, FaceTime, iCloud Mail, AirDrop, shared albums, and notes. For Microsoft, it covers messaging, calling, and work services.

If the companies refuse to cooperate with the FSB, they face large fines in Russia and eventual blocking.

Secure kernel, the VLT1 kernel uses the same way to work than the regular kernel (VLT0). VTL0 works via syscalls. In VLT1, the syscalls are named Secure Calls. 

Usermode -> syscall -> ntoskrnl.exe (VTL0) → HvlpVtlCall → VMCALL → hypervisor → securekernel.exe (VTL1)

RT @pilvar222: We ran Kimi K3.1 Pro on our cybersecurity benchmark, it's super precise (4.2% false positives), but it doesn't find as many vulnerabilities as other models

- At pass@3, it found 26/32 CVEs (81.3%), tying Opus 5. Still behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (87.5%)

- Only 4.2% of what it reports are false positives (95.8% precision), the 4th lowest rate on the benchmark. DeepSeek is at ~14%, so you get roughly 3x less noise

- Cost: $16.14 per CVE found, 8x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra ($135.23), which has a similar false positive rate

1/3 🧵

quotedTweet.rawContent:
🔐 ⚠️ phpMyAdmin 5.2.3 - 2FA Bypass! 0day++! ⚠️ 🔐 

🚨 WebAuthn signatures are parsed but never COSE-verified against credentialPublicKey 🚨 Arbitrary bytes pass the structural checks, so 2FA falls over after password auth 💀

Exploit:
> CWE-347/287 ⚠️ CVSS 8.1
> 🐙 https://t.co/ma6OkI0sOF

🧩 Root cause: web-auth/webauthn-lib is only a dev/suggest dependency 📦 The distributed tarball is built with `composer install --no-dev`, so `WebAuthn::createServer` instantiates `CustomServer` instead of `WebauthnLibServer` 👀

🔍 How? 🤦‍♂️ `CustomServer::parseAndValidateAssertionResponse` enforces structural checks only: clientData type, session challenge, origin host, rpIdHash, user-present, allowed credential id 📋 `response.signature` is decoded and never verified ❌ `credentialPublicKey` is never read 🕳️

💥 Impact: a well-formed assertion carrying correct structural fields and an arbitrary signature yields a full authenticated session 🔓 Impact is unauthorized database access through the application, not host-level code execution 🗄️
